rows.question: Can the Route10 power both of its PoE+ ports at the full 30 W per port at the same time?
rows.expected: No: 2 ports x 30 W = 60 W, but the Route10 PoE budget is 40 W
rows.answer:
No, the Route10 cannot power both PoE+ ports at a full 30 W each at the same time, because its total PoE budget is 40W. [4][7] Two ports at 30 W would need 30 W + 30 W = 60 W, which is 20 W more than the 40W budget. [4] Each of the two PoE+ ports (ports 2 and 3) is specified as 802.3at PoE+ at 54VDC, 0.6A max. [1][2]

**Not found in your documents:** The datasheet evidence does not state an explicit 30 W per-port figure; 30 W is taken from the question's premise.

rows.question: Both fall detection papers use an ESP32. How does each one send its sensor data?
rows.expected: Adebesin et al.: the ESP32 sends over LoRa to a gateway; bathroom study: ESP32-C3 nodes send 2.56 s windows over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B
rows.answer: In the wearable fall detection paper (adebesin2026), the ESP32 sends acceleration and velocity readings to the gateway over LoRa, using the RYLR896 UART LoRa transceiver module (868/915 MHz). [1] Its protocol stack runs CoAP over UDP over IPv6/6LoWPAN on LoRa, and the device responds with sensor data via CoAP, which the gateway translates to HTTP for the application. [2][3] In the bathroom fall detection paper (arXiv 2603.17069), the ESP32-C3 nodes send buffered 2.56 s windows of sensor data over Wi-Fi to a Raspberry Pi 4B edge gateway. [4] The bathroom paper's passages name no specific application-layer protocol such as MQTT, UDP or TCP. [5]

rows.question: On the Raspberry Pi 4B, how does the end-to-end latency of the radar-only model compare with the radar and vibration fusion model in the bathroom study?
rows.expected: Radar only 28.4 ms vs fusion 15.8 ms
rows.answer: On the Raspberry Pi 4B in arxiv2603.17069, the radar-only Motion-Mamba model has an end-to-end latency of 28.4 ms (7.5 ms preprocessing + 19.8 ms inference). [1] The radar and vibration fusion model has an end-to-end latency of 15.8 ms (8.9 ms preprocessing + 6.7 ms inference). [2] The fusion model is therefore faster by 28.4 ms - 15.8 ms = 12.6 ms, which is about 44% lower latency (15.8/28.4 ≈ 0.56). [1][2]

rows.question: In the bathroom study, how much energy per 2.56 s window do the radar sensing node and the vibration sensing node use?
rows.expected: Radar node (ESP32-C3 + C4001) 4740 mJ; vibration node (ESP32-C3 + ADXL345) 820 mJ
rows.answer: In the bathroom fall mmWave paper (arxiv 2603.17069), the ESP32-C3 + C4001 radar sensing node uses 4740 mJ per 2.56 s window, at an average power of 1.85 W. [1] The ESP32-C3 + ADXL345 vibration sensing node uses 820 mJ per 2.56 s window, at an average power of 0.32 W. [2] Together the two nodes use 4740 mJ (radar) + 820 mJ (vibration) = 5560 mJ per 2.56 s window. [1][2]

rows.question: Adebesin et al. cite an mmWave radar fall detection accuracy in their literature review. How does it compare with the accuracy of the full model in the bathroom study?
rows.expected: 92.3% (cited mmWave radar work, ref [10]) vs 96.1% (bathroom full model)
rows.answer: Adebesin et al. 2026 cite mmWave radar systems (ref) pairing SVM and CNN models that reach 92.3% fall detection accuracy without wearables. [1] The full two-stream model in the bathroom study (arXiv 2603.17069) reaches 96.1% window-level accuracy on the test split. [2] The bathroom model is therefore 96.1% - 92.3% = 3.8 percentage points more accurate than the cited mmWave radar system. [1][2]
